chapters.title: Chapter 3: How Property Makes and Loses Money

lessons.title: The Two Engines of Return: Rental Yield and Capital Appreciation

children.text: Between 2019 and mid-2026, average home prices in Noida rose about 125%, according to ANAROCK. Over the same period, Bengaluru prices rose about 90%, but Bengaluru's rental yield ended higher. So which city made investors more money? The honest answer is: it depends on which engine you were counting on. Property returns come from two separate engines, rent and appreciation, and they behave very differently. In Chapter 1 you learned the basic formulas. This lesson takes each engine apart properly.

body.text: Rent is the engine you can measure on the day you buy. Appreciation is the engine you can only hope for. The price you pay decides how much work each engine has to do.

children.text: Engine 1: Rental Yield, From Gross to What You Actually Keep

markDefs.definition: The share of the year a property earns no rent because it is between tenants. One month empty in a year is a vacancy rate of about 8%.

children.text: The yield a broker quotes is almost always gross yield: annual rent divided by price. What lands in your bank account is much smaller, after
vacancy
, brokerage, maintenance, property tax, repairs and income tax. Let us take one flat all the way down.
Sanjay owns a 2BHK in Gachibowli, Hyderabad, worth ₹1.1 crore. It rents for ₹35,000 a month. He is in the 30% tax slab.

body.caption: From gross to after-tax yield on Sanjay's Gachibowli flat (illustrative)

cells: Less: brokerage (half a month's rent every 2 years)
Less: society maintenance at ₹5,000 a month

markDefs.definition: Rent received in the year minus municipal taxes actually paid by the owner. The starting point for taxing rental income.

children.text: Rent is taxed under the head "Income from House Property." You start from the
net annual value
, then claim a flat 30% standard deduction for repairs, whether or not you actually spent that much. Society maintenance, brokerage and repair bills are not separately deductible.
Rent actually received (11 months): ₹3,85,000
Less property tax paid: ₹3,85,000 minus ₹15,000 = ₹3,70,000 net annual value
Less 30% standard deduction: ₹3,70,000 × 30% = ₹1,11,000, leaving ₹2,59,000 taxable
This ignores home loan interest, which can reduce the tax if the flat was bought with a loan. You will see how in Chapter 6.

body.caption: If you start from rent actually received for the months the flat was let, vacancy is already counted; do not deduct it twice.

body.text: A 3.82% gross yield became 1.79% after costs and tax. That is less than half. Whenever you compare property rent with an FD or a REIT distribution, compare net with net. A bank FD's interest is also taxed at your slab rate, but it has no vacancy, no maintenance and no painting bill.

body.title: Find the net yield
body.prompt: A flat in Kalyani Nagar, Pune is worth ₹80 lakh and rents for ₹25,000 a month. It stays empty for 1 month a year, and the owner pays ₹70,000 a year in maintenance, property tax and repairs combined. What is its net yield before income tax, in %? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: Rent received: 11 × ₹25,000 = ₹2,75,000. Less costs: ₹2,75,000 minus ₹70,000 = ₹2,05,000. Net yield: ₹2,05,000 ÷ ₹80,00,000 = 2.56%. The gross yield was 3.75%, so costs and one month of vacancy took away almost a third.

children.text: Engine 2: Capital Appreciation
Appreciation is the rise in what a buyer will pay for your property. It is not one force but several, and most of them are outside your control:
Incomes and jobs:
rising salaries near job hubs let buyers pay more.
Infrastructure:
a metro station, expressway or airport can reprice an entire corridor, usually well before it opens.
Supply:
areas where land is scarce or approvals are slow see stronger price growth than areas flooded with new launches.
Interest rates:
lower home loan rates raise how much buyers can borrow, which supports prices.
Construction costs:
when cement, steel and labour get costlier, new flats cost more, which lifts the value of existing ones.
Sentiment:
in booms, buyers chase prices up; in slumps, deals simply stop.

body.title: Average home prices, 2019 vs Q2 2026 (₹ per sq ft, ANAROCK)
Annualise Noida's run
body.prompt: Noida's average price rose from ₹4,795 per sq ft in 2019 to ₹10,780 in Q2 2026. Treating this as roughly 7 years, what is the approximate annual growth rate (CAGR), in %? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: (10,780 ÷ 4,795)^(1/7) minus 1 = 2.248^(0.143) minus 1 ≈ 12.3% a year. That is an exceptional run. Remember it started from a low base after the 2014 to 2020 slump, so it should not be extrapolated forward.

body.text: Look at when this data starts. 2019 sits near the end of a long, flat period for Indian housing, especially in Delhi-NCR. Prices had room to catch up, and low interest rates after COVID poured fuel on the recovery. Returns measured from a slump to a boom always look spectacular. The same cities measured from 2011 to 2019 would tell a very different story.

children.text: When Both Engines Run at Once: Why Yields Rose

Normally, when prices jump, yields fall, because rent does not keep up. Between 2019 and 2026, the opposite happened in all four cities: yields rose even as prices nearly doubled. That can only happen if rents grew even faster than prices. Return-to-office hiring, GCC expansion and people postponing home purchases all pushed rents up sharply after 2021.

markDefs.definition: A property's price divided by its annual rent. It tells you how many years of rent it would take to pay the purchase price, and is the inverse of gross yield.

children.text: A quick way to compare rent and price across cities is the
price-to-rent ratio
. It works like a P/E ratio for property: the higher it is, the more you are paying for each rupee of rent, and the more your return depends on appreciation.

body.caption: A 4% gross yield means a price-to-rent ratio of 25: the price equals 25 years of rent.
Price-to-rent ratios implied by Q2 2026 yields (ANAROCK)
headers: Years of rent to repay the price

body.title: Flip the ratio
body.textWithBlank: A flat with a price-to-rent ratio of 25 has a gross rental yield of ___%.
body.explanation: Gross yield = 100 ÷ price-to-rent ratio = 100 ÷ 25 = 4%. The two numbers always describe the same relationship between price and rent, from opposite sides.

body.title: Two ways to invest in property

columns.label: Yield-led investing
points: Buy where rent is high relative to price, near established job hubs
Most of the return is known on day one
Less dependent on the market going up

columns.label: Appreciation-led investing
points: Buy in emerging corridors ahead of infrastructure or job growth
Most of the return depends on a future buyer paying more
Can deliver large gains if the story plays out
Can go nowhere for years if it does not, while rent barely covers costs

body.label: The break-even question
body.value: At a 2% net yield, you need about 6% appreciation just to match an 8% return
body.context: Before you buy, work out how much appreciation you need each year to beat simpler alternatives. If that number looks optimistic for the area, the property is priced for a story, not for its rent.

body.title: Which engine can you count on?
body.question: On the day you buy a rented flat, which part of its future return can you estimate most reliably?
options: Capital appreciation, because past price growth shows the trend
Rental yield, because the current rent and your costs are known today
Neither can be estimated at all
body.explanation: Current rent, maintenance and property tax are known facts on the day you buy, so net yield can be estimated with reasonable confidence. Appreciation depends on future jobs, supply, interest rates and sentiment, none of which past price growth guarantees.

body.title: Kondapur or Sector 150?
body.scenario: Divya has ₹1.2 crore to invest and is choosing between two flats. Option A is in Kondapur, Hyderabad, close to established IT offices, with a 2.6% net yield before tax. Option B is in Noida Sector 150, with a 2.0% net yield. The Noida broker says: "Noida prices went up 125% since 2019. You will easily make 12% a year here."
body.prompt: How should Divya think about these two options using the two engines of return?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Separate the engines: A offers 2.6% net yield, B offers 2.0%. On the rent engine alone, A is ahead by 0.6 percentage points a year, or about ₹72,000 a year on ₹1.2 crore.
2. Test the appreciation claim: 125% since 2019 is about 12% a year, but it was measured from the bottom of a long slump to a strong upcycle. Past growth from a low base is not a forecast.
3. Work out break-even: to match A, B needs appreciation 0.6 percentage points a year higher than A's. If both areas grow similarly, A wins.
4. Check the drivers: for B, what completed infrastructure and job hubs support demand, and how much new supply is coming? For A, how deep and stable is the tenant base?
5. Price-to-rent: B's lower yield means Divya pays more years of rent for the same flat, so more of her return depends on a future buyer.
6. Reasonable conclusion: unless Divya has strong, specific reasons to expect faster appreciation in Sector 150, the Kondapur flat offers a return she can see today. Either way, she should model a range of appreciation outcomes, including 0% to 3% a year, not just the broker's 12%.

body.title: Sizing Up Both Engines Before You Buy
steps: Get actual rents for three to five similar flats nearby, not the broker's estimate
Build a net yield: subtract vacancy, maintenance, property tax, repairs and brokerage
Estimate tax on rent at your slab rate after the 30% standard deduction
Calculate the price-to-rent ratio and compare it with nearby areas
Convert any past price growth claim into a CAGR and check its start date
Work out the annual appreciation you need to beat an FD, index fund or REIT

body.label: Magicbricks: Rent Listings
body.description: Check current asking rents for comparable flats in your target locality before trusting any yield estimate.

cards.definition: Annual rent divided by property price, before any costs, vacancy or tax.
Rent actually received minus owner's costs, divided by price. What you really earn from rent.
Time a property earns no rent between tenants. One month a year is about 8%.
Rent received minus municipal taxes paid; the base for taxing rental income.
A flat deduction on net annual value for rental income, allowed regardless of actual repair spending.
Price divided by annual rent. Equal to 100 divided by gross yield; higher means more reliance on appreciation.
The increase in what buyers will pay for a property, driven by jobs, infrastructure, supply, rates and sentiment.

points: Property returns come from two engines: rent, which you can measure today, and appreciation, which you can only estimate.
Gross yield overstates reality: in our Gachibowli example, 3.82% gross became 2.53% net and 1.79% after tax.
Rental income is taxed after a flat 30% standard deduction on net annual value, at your slab rate.
ANAROCK data shows Noida up 125% and Bengaluru up 90% from 2019 to Q2 2026, with yields rising too because rents grew faster than prices.
The price-to-rent ratio (100 ÷ gross yield) shows how much of your return depends on appreciation.
Before buying, calculate the appreciation you need to beat simpler alternatives, and question any forecast built on a slump-to-boom period.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment or tax advice. City data comes from ANAROCK and Magicbricks research, and actual rents, costs and prices vary by project and locality. Tax treatment depends on your circumstances and current law. Consult a tax professional and a SEBI-registered investment adviser before making investment decisions.
